newsitem.title: USA: Strong dollar may hurt US meat sales but not grain.
newsitem.headline: Strong dollar may hurt US meat sales but not grain.

text.p: The strong U.S. dollar is tempering demand for U.S. meat exports, but does not appear to be curbing the appetite of foreign buyers of U.S. grain and oilseeds, commodity market analysts said.
"I believe the dollar has slowed U.S. exports, especially of high quality beef," said Kansas State University professor Joe Arata.
Tight stocks of grains and oilseeds, however, are so far overriding potential strong dollar declines in exports.

"Stocks are tight. Grain is in tremendous demand, so you won't notice (dollar strength). It will be overwhelmed by other supply and demand factors," said Paul Prentice, president of Farm Sector Economics Inc, an agricultural consulting firm based in Colorado Springs, Colo.
The dollar has risen 15 percent against the yen in the past 12 months, about 10 percent in 1997 alone. It rose to 127 yen Wednesday for the first time since August 1992.

"In my view even that relationship of the strong dollar and the flow of exports has been eroded in this current era of relatively tight grain stocks and strong global economic growth," said Refco Global Research analyst, Rich Feltes.
U.S. farm exports totaled a record $59.8 billion in fiscal 1996, or about six percent of total exports of goods and services.
Feltes said studies had shown the past relationship between dollar movements and exports was much stronger in oilseeds than in corn or wheat.
But strong global demand and tight supplies of oilseeds minimizes the potential dollar impact on U.S. soybean and soymeal shipments this year.
Feltes said studies also suggest a lag of eight months or more between a major currency move and any impact on exports. Prentice said the lag could be as long as three years.
Analysts said U.S. corn was largely exempt from currency considerations at this time of year due to the lack of competition from other suppliers.
"The U.S. has a tendency, particularly at this time of year, to be the only game in town," said Mike Helmar, senior economist, agricultural services, for the WEFA Group.
In the meat sector, Arata said the impact would be greater on beef than pork exports as they are more expensive and price sensitive.

"We are the source of high quality beef to southeast Asia and by the time it gets to the consumer it is very expensive," Arata said. "We are making it more expensive (due to dollar strength). They would buy a lot more if they could get it at a lower price."
